query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating 1.5 at.% Aluminum into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr via arc melting followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) will induce the formation of a continuous, self-healing Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby overcoming the alloy's poor oxygen resistance while maintaining its high-temperature yield strength and ductility through the sluggish diffusion kinetics of the refractory matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) structure, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffering from rapid oxidation and scale spallation in air.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1.5 at.% Aluminum (Al) to the alloy composition, followed by arc melting for homogeneity and Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C under 207 MPa for 1 hour to eliminate porosity and refine the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours; mechanical testing at 1000 °C with strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent, and self-healing Al2O3 (alumina) oxide scale formed on the surface, stabilized by the sluggish diffusion kinetics of the HfNbTaTiZr matrix which prevents rapid oxygen ingress and scale spallation.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen and preferentially oxidizes to form a dense, protective Al2O3 layer. The high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion in the HfNbTaTiZr matrix retard the growth rate of this oxide scale and prevent the formation of volatile oxides (like HfO2 or Nb2O5) that typically cause spallation in unalloyed RHEAs. The Al addition does not significantly degrade the BCC matrix strength due to the solid solution strengthening effect and the retention of the single-phase structure at this low concentration.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-modified HfNbTaTiZr alloy will exhibit a mass gain rate at 1000 °C reduced by at least one order of magnitude compared to the untreated cast alloy, with no significant loss in yield strength (remaining >150 MPa) or ductility (>10%) at 1000 °C, effectively enabling practical high-temperature use in oxidizing atmospheres.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which forms non-protective, porous, and spalling oxide scales (primarily HfO2 and Nb2O5) leading to rapid degradation and loss of mechanical integrity in air at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for Al additions between 0.5 and 3.0 at.%; higher Al content (>3 at.%) may risk the formation of brittle intermetallic phases (e.g., Laves phases or B2 precipitates) that could compromise ductility, while lower content may fail to form a continuous protective scale.
generation.uncertainty: While Al is known to improve oxidation resistance in RHEAs (PMC7513042), the specific interaction of Al with the HfNbTaTiZr system to form a stable Al2O3 scale without inducing detrimental phase separation or embrittlement at 1.5 at.% is not explicitly confirmed in the provided evidence for this specific composition. The exact threshold for maintaining ductility while achieving full oxidation protection is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 1.5 at.% Al added and processed via arc melting + HIP (1200 °C, 207 MPa, 1 h); (2) Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. Expose both to static air at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Subsequently, perform tensile tests at 1000 °C (strain rate 10^-3 s^-1) and measure mass gain.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and composition via Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS)
Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm^2) after 100 hours
Yield strength (MPa) and tensile ductility (%) at 1000 °C
Phase identification via X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to check for brittle intermetallic formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Al-modified sample shows a mass gain rate within 50% of the untreated sample (indicating no protective scale) OR if the yield strength drops below 100 MPa or ductility falls below 5% due to the formation of brittle Al-rich intermetallic phases.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
